opus-5.5.text:
So the way I like to put it is that most of what we call "taste" is actually smell. Your tongue is doing real work, but it's a pretty low-dimensional sensor. You've got sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami, and maybe a couple of others people argue about, like fat or a kind of metallic or starchy sense. That's a handful of channels. Your nose, by contrast, has around 400 different types of olfactory receptors in humans, and they're combinatorially activated, so the space of things you can perceive through smell is enormous.

When you're eating, a lot of the volatile molecules from the food travel up the back of your throat into your nasal cavity. That's called retronasal olfaction, as opposed to orthonasal, which is sniffing from the outside. Your brain doesn't really label that signal as "smell." It fuses it with what's happening on your tongue, plus texture, temperature, and even the sound of crunching, and presents it to you as a single unified percept that we call flavor. And we attribute the whole thing to the mouth.

The easy demonstration is to pinch your nose and eat a jelly bean. You'll get sweet, maybe a little sour, but you won't know if it's cherry or cinnamon or lemon. Then you let go of your nose, and suddenly the flavor sort of blooms. That moment is the retronasal smell coming online. It's also why food tastes so flat when you have a cold.

People often cite a number like 80% of flavor coming from smell. I'd treat that figure loosely, because it's hard to define what a percentage of a perception even means. But directionally it's right. If you want to understand why a strawberry tastes like a strawberry, or why coffee tastes like coffee, the answer is mostly in the volatile chemistry and in the nose. The tongue tells you whether it's sweet or bitter. The nose tells you what it is.

For those of us working on machine learning for olfaction, that's part of what makes this exciting. If you can model how molecular structure maps to smell perception, you're not just modeling perfume, you're getting at a huge part of how we experience food.

r001.rationale: Explains that volatile food molecules travel from the mouth up the back of the throat into the nasal cavity during eating and names this retronasal olfaction.

r002.rationale: Cites a loose figure of 80% of flavor coming from smell, not approximately 90% smell and 10% taste.

r003.rationale: Describes the tongue as a low-dimensional sensor with a handful of taste channels, contrasted with the nose's roughly 400 receptor types and much larger perceptual space.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite things to talk about, because almost everybody gets it backwards. When people say "taste," what they're actually describing, most of the time, is smell. Your tongue is a pretty crude instrument. It gives you sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami, maybe a couple of others that are still being debated. That's it. That's the whole vocabulary of taste. Everything else — the difference between a strawberry and a raspberry, the difference between a cabernet and a pinot, the difference between cinnamon and clove — that's smell.

And the reason it feels like it's coming from your mouth is because of something called retronasal olfaction. When you chew and swallow, volatile molecules get pushed up the back of your throat into your nasal cavity, and they hit the same olfactory receptors as when you sniff something. But your brain does this trick where it localizes the sensation to your mouth, because that's where the food is. So you experience it as "taste," but the information is coming through your nose.

The classic demonstration is to pinch your nose shut and eat a jellybean. You'll get sweet, and that's about it. Then you let go of your nose and suddenly, boom, it's cherry, or it's lime. All of that flavor identity was olfactory the whole time. Or think about what food is like when you have a bad cold — people say they can't taste anything, but their tongue is working fine. They've lost smell.

So if you were to put rough numbers on it, and I'd say this with the caveat that it's not a clean decomposition, the majority of what we call flavor is olfactory. Taste gives you the basic hedonic scaffolding — is this nutritious, is this dangerous — and smell fills in essentially all of the detail. There's also texture and temperature and chemesthesis, things like the burn of chili or the cooling of menthol, which are a third channel through the trigeminal system. But the richness, the specificity, the thing that lets you tell thousands of foods apart — that's smell.

And that's part of why I find olfaction so compelling as a scientific problem. It's doing this enormous amount of work in our everyday experience, and yet it's the sense we understand the least and have the worst tools for.

r001.rationale: It explains that chewing and swallowing push volatile molecules from the mouth up the throat into the nasal cavity and names this retronasal olfaction.

r002.rationale: It says smell contributes the majority of flavor but gives no 90%/10% estimate.

r003.rationale: It describes taste as a crude instrument limited to a few basic qualities, while smell supplies flavor detail and specificity.

astra-6.text:
I think the easiest way to understand it is to distinguish taste from flavor. Taste is what your tongue detects—sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. But much of the detail that makes one food different from another comes from smell.

When you chew, volatile molecules travel from the back of your mouth up into your nose. That’s called retronasal olfaction, and your brain combines it with taste and sensations like temperature and texture into this unified experience of flavor. You don’t usually experience it as smelling; you experience it as something happening in your mouth.

So if you hold your nose while eating something, you can still tell that it’s sweet or sour, but it becomes much harder to identify its particular flavor. Release your nose, and suddenly that identity comes back. I’d be cautious about assigning a precise percentage to smell versus taste, because it depends on the food and what you’re measuring. But smell contributes an enormous amount of the richness and specificity.

r001.rationale: It explains that volatile molecules travel from the back of the mouth into the nose during chewing and names this retronasal olfaction.

r002.rationale: It explicitly declines to assign a precise percentage and gives no 90%/10% estimate.

r003.rationale: It says smell provides much of flavor’s detail and specificity, but does not clearly characterize taste as less complex in sensory dimensionality.

sol-6.1.text:
Taste and smell are distinct senses that your brain combines into what we call flavor. Taste gives you things like sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. Smell provides much of the identity and complexity: Is this strawberry or raspberry? Is this coffee or chocolate?

When you chew, volatile molecules travel from your mouth up into your nose through the back of your throat. That’s called retronasal olfaction, and your brain tends to locate that experience in your mouth, so you think you’re tasting it. A simple way to experience the distinction is to hold your nose while eating a jelly bean. You’ll get sweetness, but when you release your nose, suddenly the particular flavor appears.

So smell contributes enormously, but I’d be careful about assigning a single percentage. Flavor also includes texture, temperature, and sensations like the burn of chili peppers. It’s a combined experience.

r001.rationale: It explains that volatile molecules travel from the mouth up into the nose during chewing and names this retronasal olfaction.

r002.rationale: It gives no 90%/10% estimate and explicitly cautions against assigning a single percentage.

r003.rationale: It presents taste as a set of basic qualities and says smell supplies much of flavor’s identity and complexity, characterizing smell as more complex.
